samasa.sense: the blow Raktabīja aimed at Caṇḍikā (8.57)

morph.note: Perfect ātmanepada of √कृ: reduplicated च-क्र्-, ending -ए. वेदनां चक्रे ‘caused pain’.
अल्प ‘small’ with the diminutive -क and feminine -आ (the a before क becomes i): अल्पिका ‘a little’. न … अल्पिकाम् अपि: ‘not even the slightest’.

mantras.anvaya: गदापातः च अस्याः अल्पिकाम् अपि वेदनां न चक्रे; आहतस्य तस्य देहात् तु बहु शोणितं सुस्राव।
mantras.lit: And the blow of the mace did not cause her even slight pain; but from the body of him, struck, much blood flowed.
mantras.tr: His mace-blow caused her not the slightest pain, while from his wounded body the blood poured out.

comm.t: The contrast is the point: his strongest blow does nothing to Caṇḍikā, while her blow (8.56) makes him bleed. The second line repeats the words of 8.43 (बहु सुस्राव शोणितम्), but this time the blood has somewhere else to go.

samasa.sense: from the blood as it fell into her mouth

morph.note: Present of सम् + प्रति + √इष् (stem इच्छ-), used for past narrative (historic present). It fulfils Caṇḍikā’s command प्रतीच्छ (8.54).
Neuter accusative pronoun ‘it’, taking up शोणितम्. It could also be the first member of a compound तद्वक्त्रेण ‘with that mouth’ (8.54 वक्त्रेणानेन); see Uncertain.

mantras.anvaya: चामुण्डा यतः ततः तत् (शोणितं) वक्त्रेण सम्प्रतीच्छति; रक्तपातात् अस्याः मुखे ये महासुराः समुद्गताः, (तान् …)
mantras.anvaya_en: A main clause, then a relative clause whose correlative (तान्) opens 8.60.
mantras.lit: From wherever (it flowed), Cāmuṇḍā caught it with her mouth; the great asuras who arose in her mouth from the falling blood —
mantras.tr: Wherever it flowed, Cāmuṇḍā caught the blood in her mouth; and the great asuras who sprang up in her mouth from that blood —

comm.t: Kālī is now called Cāmuṇḍā by the narrator. She catches every stream of blood (यतस्ततः ‘from wherever’), and even the asuras that still form from it are born inside her mouth.

flags.uncertain: तद्वक्त्रेण: taken as two words, तत् (the blood, object of सम्प्रतीच्छति) + वक्त्रेण. A compound तद्वक्त्रेण ‘with that mouth’ is possible; the verb then lacks a stated object, so the two-word reading is preferred.

morph.note: Perfect of √पा ‘drink’: reduplicated प-पौ, with the ending -औ that ā-roots take in the first and third singular.
The subject of the next verse’s verb (8.61 जघान). The second line of this verse lists her weapons and leaves the verb for the next.

mantras.anvaya: अथ चामुण्डा तान् चखाद, तस्य शोणितं च पपौ। देवी शूलेन वज्रेण बाणैः असिभिः ऋष्टिभिः (8.61: तं रक्तबीजं जघान)।
mantras.anvaya_en: The first line closes the sentence begun in 8.59; the second line opens a new sentence completed in 8.61.
mantras.lit: — them Cāmuṇḍā then devoured, and drank his blood. The Goddess, with spear, thunderbolt, arrows, swords and double-edged swords …
mantras.tr: — Cāmuṇḍā devoured them, and drank his blood. Then the Goddess, with spear and thunderbolt, with arrows, swords and double-edged blades …
mantras.tr_note: The second line is completed by 8.61.

comm.t: Cāmuṇḍā does both things Caṇḍikā asked: she eats the asuras born of the blood and drinks the blood itself. Meanwhile the Goddess attacks with every weapon at once.

Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has the names महाग्रासा (752) and महाशना (753), ‘great devourer’ and ‘great eater’, beside महाकाली (751). They name in general terms the power Cāmuṇḍā shows here; the two texts are separate works.

on the back of the earth

samasa.sense: cut down by all the weapons together

morph.note: पीत is the past participle of √पा ‘drink’. The bahuvrīhi carries the whole explanation of his death in one word: his blood was drunk, so no new asura could rise.
Perfect of √पत् with the reduplicated syllable प- (contrast the unreduplicated plural पेतुः, 8.35).

mantras.anvaya: (देवी) चामुण्डापीतशोणितं तं रक्तबीजं जघान; शस्त्रसङ्घसमाहतः सः महीपृष्ठे पपात।
mantras.lit: (The Goddess) struck down that Raktabīja, whose blood had been drunk by Cāmuṇḍā. Struck by the mass of weapons, he fell on the surface of the earth,
mantras.tr: struck down Raktabīja, whose blood Cāmuṇḍā had drunk. Smitten by that host of weapons, he fell to the ground,
mantras.tr_note: The first line completes the sentence begun in 8.60; the second runs on into 8.62.

comm.t: The death of Raktabīja. Each detail matters: the blood had been drunk, so the many weapons that had multiplied him before now kill him.

samasa.literal: he from whom the blood has gone out

samasa.vigraha: न विद्यते तुला यस्य सः, तम्

samasa.literal: those whose number is thrice ten
samasa.sense: the gods, by the round number for the thirty-three
samasa.alt: A traditional etymology reads तिस्रः दशाः (अवस्थाः) येषां ते, ‘those who have (only) three stages of life’ (without old age). The numerical reading is the usual one.

morph.note: Perfect of अव + √आप्: the perfect of √आप् is आप- (आपुः ‘they obtained’); with अव, अवापुः.
Vocative: Medhas, the narrator, turns to King Suratha. नृप at the end of the line is a second vocative to the same listener.

mantras.anvaya: महीपाल, (सः) रक्तबीजः महासुरः नीरक्तः च (पपात)। नृप, ततः ते त्रिदशाः अतुलं हर्षम् अवापुः।
mantras.anvaya_en: The first line completes 8.61 (सः पपात); the second is a new sentence.
mantras.lit: — and bloodless, O protector of the earth, the great asura Raktabīja. Then those gods attained incomparable joy, O king.
mantras.tr: drained of his blood, O lord of the earth — Raktabīja, the great asura. Then the gods, O king, were filled with boundless joy.

comm.t: Medhas, the sage telling the story, addresses King Suratha twice (महीपाल, नृप), marking the turn of the episode. The gods, afraid in 8.52, now rejoice.

samasa.type: tṛtīyā tatpuruṣa containing a ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa (असृङ्मद)
samasa.literal: exalted by the intoxication of blood
samasa.sense: frenzied with the blood they had drunk

morph.note: Perfect of √नृत्: reduplicated न-नर्त, with guṇa of ṛ to ar in the singular.
उद्धत is the past participle of उद् + √हन् (‘raised up’, hence ‘wild, unrestrained’). असृज् ‘blood’ is the same noun as in 8.52.

mantras.anvaya_en: A single clause; the genitive तेषाम् is taken with जातः.
mantras.lit: The band of Mothers born of them danced, wild with the intoxication of blood.
mantras.tr: And the band of Mothers born from the gods danced, wild with the blood they had drunk.
mantras.tr_note: ‘From the gods’ makes तेषाम् explicit; ‘they had drunk’ interprets असृङ्मद ‘intoxication of blood’.

comm.t: The chapter ends with the Mothers’ victory dance. तेषाम् recalls their origin: they came out of the bodies of the gods (8.13). This last mantra is a half-śloka; in recitation it carries the closing bīja ॐ, which belongs to the pāṭha, not to the verse.
The Mothers return to fight beside the Goddess in the next chapter (9.8 कृत्वा युद्धं तु मातृभिः) and are praised one by one in the hymn of chapter 11 (11.13–20).

flags.uncertain: तेषाम् could also be read with the whole clause (‘their band of Mothers’, i.e. the gods’ own), or as ‘among them (the gods)’. Taking it with जातः, ‘born of them’, agrees with 8.13.
